Weaver61; 1:500, overnight at 4 °C). For pan-epithelial (pan-EPI) cocktail staining, the antibodies (Abcam, ab7753; Invitrogen, MA5-13156; and BD Biosciences, 610182) were combined, each at 1:200, and applied for 2 h at room temperature.

Immunofluorescence staining and imaging of TMAs was performed as previously described60 for pan-cadherin antibodies to label the tumour cells and their plasma membranes and the nuclear marker DAPI.

Preprocessing and segmentation were performed essentially as described previously36. In brief, TMA cores were de-arrayed using built-in tools from QuPath (v.0.5.1)62. Cores exhibiting folding artifacts, blurriness or limited tumour content were excluded from analysis. After preprocessing, nuclei were segmented based on DAPI signal using custom-trained Cellpose 2.0 models (v.2.0 and v.2.2.2)63, separately optimized for the TMA and whole-slide image datasets. The tumour and stromal compartments were identified using a multi-label U-Net trained on 30 representative cores. Pixel-level annotations were generated manually in ilastik (v.1.4.0)64 based on pan-EPI staining.

Tumour architectural subtypes were classified through a transfer-learning pipeline comprising four stages:.

Stage 1, tiling: each TMA core image was subdivided into non-overlapping 448 × 448 px (208 × 208 µm) tiles covering the full tissue area.

Recent findings suggest that stage 2, feature embedding: a multi-label U-Net was trained to segment architectural subtypes. Ground-truth masks were derived from the tumour–stroma segmentations described above, with tumour regions manually re-annotated according to three architectural subtypes: glandular (organized, lumen-forming structures), fragmented (disrupted tumour clusters) and solid (dense). Two additional classes (stroma and edge/background) were included to handle non-tumour regions. The training set comprised 196 cores selected as unambiguous archetypes of each architectural subtype. The validity of this selection was assessed by computing silhouette scores on a panel of interpretable morphological features (Fig. 1f) and comparing the archetype score to a null distribution generated from 1,000 size-matched random draws of cohort cores assigned matching per-class labels (Extended Data Fig. 2e). Each tile was then passed through the trained U-Net, and the activations at the deepest convolutional layer (bottleneck) were aggregated through global average pooling to yield a compact feature vector per tile, encoding the dominant morphological pattern without requiring a separate hand-crafted feature design.

Stage 3, tile-level classification: a multinomial logistic regression classifier (L-BFGS solver, scikit-learn) was trained on the bottleneck embeddings to assign each tile to one of five classes: glandular, fragmented, solid, stroma or edge/background. Features were standardized before classification. The training set comprised 1,154 manually annotated tiles (365 glandular, 251 fragmented, 148 solid, 199 stroma and 191 edge/background), randomly sampled from 760 cores across the cohort. Performance was evaluated using stratified fivefold cross-validation. At inference, the classifier output five class probabilities per tile; tiles dominated by edge or stroma (probability ≥ 0.5) were excluded, and the remaining glandular, fragmented and solid probabilities were renormalized to sum to one before assigning each tile to its most probable architectural subtype (argmax).

Stage 4, patient-level classification: tile-level predictions were aggregated per sample. The proportion of tumour-classified tiles belonging to each architectural subtype was computed separately for the CT (centre of the tumour) and IM. If a single subtype accounted for more than 50% of tiles, the sample was classified as that dominant architecture; otherwise, it was labelled mixed. The trained U-Net can be reused to extract morphological embeddings from other colorectal cancer datasets, provided that a membrane staining is available and that tissue tiles are of comparable physical size to those used in this study (448 × 448 pixels, corresponding to approximately 208 × 208 µm at the imaging resolution used here); tiles acquired at a different pixel resolution can be resampled (downsampled or upsampled) to match the model’s input size. However, the tile-level logistic regression classifier generally requires retraining to account for dataset-specific differences such as staining variability, imaging conditions or cohort composition. This is the strategy that we followed when applying the pipeline to the validation and multiplex datasets in this study: the U-Net embeddings were extracted directly, while the classifier was retrained on a fresh set of annotated tiles for each dataset. For the validation dataset, the classifier was retrained by supplementing the original training set with 205 additional annotated tiles (44 glandular, 49 fragmented, 28 solid, 50 stroma and 34 edge/background). For the multiplex dataset, 1,886 tiles were independently annotated (740 glandular, 446 fragmented, 123 solid, 491 stroma and 86 edge/background) and used to train a separate classifier. The pretrained U-Net model is available in ONNX format at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20343193).

Branch lengths were quantified from the binary tumour mask by first removing small objects (<20 px) and filling small holes (<100 px area), then skeletonizing the mask using skimage.morphology.skeletonize. Small spurious branches with an arc length of shorter than 5 pixels were removed by pruning using the skan library. Branch lengths were measured as geodesic arc lengths along the skeleton paths (√2-weighted pixel distances) using skan.summarize()[‘branch-distance’].

Recent findings suggest that the global contour roughness of the tumour boundary was assessed by extracting all contours from the binary tumour mask at level 0.5 using skimage.measure.find_contours. Contours with fewer than five points were discarded. The remaining contours were smoothed with a Gaussian filter (σ = 1) to reduce pixel noise. Pointwise curvature κ for a smoothed contour (x(s), y(s)) was computed by finite differences:.

where primes denote derivatives with respect to the contour parameter. Absolute curvature values were summed over all contours and normalized by the total number of contour points N to yield mean roughness per unit length.

Lumens within the binary tumour mask were detected by filling all holes (scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes) and subtracting the original mask. The resulting lumen mask was labelled, and each lumen area (in pixels) was measured through skimage.measure.regionprops.

For each cell centroid, the Euclidean distances to its k = 3 nearest neighbours were computed using sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors with a BallTree algorithm. For each cell, the mean, s.d., coefficient of variation and maximum of the k neighbour distances were stored as features.

In a recent development, the local nuclear orientation order (Ψk) was computed for each cell using its k = 3 nearest neighbours. For each neighbour, the orientation angle θ was obtained by projecting the cell’s orientation vector (defined by its longest axis) onto a fixed reference direction. The nematic order parameter was then calculated as:.

yielding a value between 0 (random orientations) and 1 (perfectly aligned neighbours).

Stroma proximity was determined by computing, for each tumour cell centroid, the minimum Euclidean distance to the set of stroma cell centroids using pairwise distance computation (scipy.spatial.distance.cdist).

Tumour–stroma ratio was calculated by measuring the total pixel areas of the tumour and stroma compartments from the segmentation mask and computing the ratio of tumour pixel count to stroma pixel count.

Industry observers note that the fragmentation index was computed by first constructing a spatial proximity graph of all tumour cell centroids, where an edge connects any two cells of which the Euclidean distance is within 80 pixels (radius-based connectivity using a BallTree). Louvain community detection was then applied to this unweighted graph to partition cells into spatially coherent communities. The fragmentation index was calculated as the number of detected communities divided by the cell count.

Recent findings suggest that whole-core fluorescence images were segmented into 12 tissue compartments with a multi-scale tumour/stroma classifier, and tumour islands were defined as connected components of the tumour class on the cleaned compartment map after upsampling to image resolution. The stromal compartment was restricted to a strict definition that excluded muscle, vessel, adipose, dense-stroma and debris classes. For each tumour island, a peri-tumoural region of interest was constructed as the 50 µm band immediately outside the island border, intersected with the strict stroma mask. Within this region, fibre body masks were obtained for the collagen I and TNC channels (analysed independently) using a fine-tuned U-Net applied at a probability threshold of 0.5.

From each body mask, we derived three independent descriptors of the underlying fibre network65: (1) the box-counting fractal dimension of the binarized mask, capturing network roughness and branching complexity; (2) the mean structure-tensor coherence within the mask, ranging from 0 for isotropic networks to 1 for perfectly aligned fibres; and (3) the median local fibre thickness, computed as twice the Euclidean distance transform sampled along the fibre skeleton and converted to micrometres using a pixel size of 0.325 µm. Features were emitted per (image × island × channel × distance band × stroma definition × architecture) so that all downstream summaries remained traceable to the underlying islands and fluorescence pixels. To avoid within-image pseudoreplication, every subsequent comparison was performed on per-(image × architecture) means, obtained by averaging each feature across the islands sharing the same architecture within an image.

Whole-slide image immunostainings were registered using the warpy workflow in ImageJ and QuPath. Whole-slide images were subsequently divided into non-overlapping tiles of 1,000 × 1,000 pixels and selected for downstream analysis in a manner analogous to TMAs, including tumour/stroma classification and nuclear segmentation. For each nucleus, the average nuclear intensity of markers (ANXA1, SNAIL1) was quantified. For cytoplasmic markers (E-cadherin, ANXA1, VIM), the nuclear contour was dilated by 5 pixels to approximate the cytoplasmic region, from which the average cytoplasmic intensity was computed. Single-cell profiles were then clustered using the Leiden algorithm at a resolution of 0.1.

Sources indicate that for each whole-slide-image tile, we computed a spatial-coherence score that quantifies whether cells with the same label group together or segregate. First, for every cell we counted its 12 immediate closest neighbours that shared the same label and averaged this count across all cells in the tile. Next, we generated a null range by randomly shuffling the position of all cells 100 times, repeating the same neighbour counting for each shuffle; the average value from these shuffled sets was taken as the expected mean. The score was then calculated as (observed – expected_mean)/(expected_max – expected_mean). A score above zero means cells with the same label cluster together more than would be expected by chance (attraction), a value of zero corresponds to a random arrangement and a negative value denotes spatial repulsion, where same-label cells are less likely to be adjacent than expected by chance.

TMA cores were identified using the dearrayer functionality in QuPath. Background illumination correction and background subtraction were subsequently performed for each core and staining round using PyBaSiC. TMAs were registered across six staining rounds using the DAPI channel as a reference. All cores underwent semi-manual quality control to remove samples that were damaged, exhibited poor registration or contained absent/very low tumour content.

Nuclear segmentation was performed using the Cellpose cyto3 model with the DAPI channel as the input. Tissue pixels were classified into tumour, stroma, tissue fold, autofluorescence, necrosis and background using an iterative supervised approach in ilastik until good visual agreement between pan-EPI signal and tumour masks was achieved across cores. For each cell, mean marker intensities were extracted using pyradiomics, and nuclear shape features were computed using a custom Python pipeline. To approximate cytoplasmic signal, nuclear masks were expanded by three pixels using expand_labels from skimage. We also computed, for each nucleus, the mean value of the ilastik pixel-classification probability map to derive cell-level classification confidence metrics.

According to recent reports, before clustering, cells with extreme nuclear areas were removed by excluding the lowest 1st percentile and highest 99th percentile. Tumour cells were then selected based on a tumour probability threshold of >0.5 and processed using a standard Scanpy workflow. Data were scaled using scanpy.pp.scale with max_value = 10, such that values were truncated to a maximum of 10 after scaling. Principal component analysis was performed using the maximum available number of components, and a k-nearest-neighbour graph was constructed with n_neighbors = 50. Clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm with the igraph-based implementation.

According to recent reports, for patient-level grouping, normalized phenotype distributions were used as input for hierarchical clustering (Ward linkage). The number of patient groups was determined based on biological interpretability and stability of the resulting clusters.

It has been revealed that tile-level U-Net embeddings were z-scored and used to build a k-nearest-neighbour graph, visualized by t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE). Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) was computed on the three architecture classes (glandular, fragmented, solid, assigned by argmax of the renormalized U-Net probabilities after removing edge and stroma tiles) and overlaid on the t-SNE. Diffusion pseudotime was computed from a diffusion map of the same embeddings, rooted at the most confident glandular tile, and tiles were grouped into 40 equal-width pseudotime bins. Within each bin, architecture probabilities were averaged, and cell phenotype fractions (cells assigned to tiles by centroid position) were averaged and renormalized to unit sum.

Spatial transcriptomics was performed using the GeoMX-DSP platform (Nanostring/Bruker). Eight patients with stage II/III CRC were selected from the TMA cohort based on presence of architecturally heterogeneous tumours. Samples were prepared according to recommendations from the vendor for FFPE slides, including baking for 60 min at 60 °C, dewaxing and antigen retrieval with ER2 for 20 min at 100 °C, fixation in NBF (10%), incubation in NBF stop and proteinase K treatment (15 min at 37 °C). These steps were performed on the Leica BondRX autostainer. The slides were incubated with the probes overnight and, after stringent washes, were stained with Syto13, pan-cytokeratin (AF532), αSMA (custom conjugated on AF647) and CD45 (AF594) antibodies to detect tumour and stromal microenvironments. ROIs (67, 61, 96 and 59 for the four slides, carrying patients 1 and 2, 3 and 5, 4 and 6, and 7 and 8, respectively) were segmented for pan-cytokeratin positivity to collect 82, 94, 141 and 63 areas of interest (AOIs) representing tumour and tumour–stroma boundary. Each ROI yielded a tumour AOI and, where collected, a stroma AOI. Transcriptomic analyses of the tumour compartment (Figs. 2f, 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 10a) used the 249 tumour AOIs from 8 patients. After scanning, tissue sections were additionally stained with antibodies against SNAIL1 (Santa Cruz, sc-271977), E-cadherin (BD, 610182), ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486) and VIM (Santa Cruz, sc-6260) and imaged using Phenoimager (Akoya Biosciences).

In a recent development, quality control of the sequencing data was performed in R using GeoMx packages, following standard GeoMx QC guidelines. Segment filtering employed the following thresholds: minimum reads per segment (AOI) = 1,000, minimum percentage of reads trimmed = 80, minimum percentage of reads stitched = 80, minimum percentage of reads aligned = 75, minimum sequencing saturation = 50, minimum negative control counts = 1, maximum counts in the NTC (no-template control) well = 9,000.

According to recent reports, segments with low signal were removed based on the limit of quantification. Gene filtering was applied by both compartment (tumour/stroma) and architecture type to preserve important genes in underrepresented regions. A 10% segment cut-off was used. Data were normalized using the third quartile (Q3) method.

For differential gene expression, raw counts were analysed using the PyDESeq2 Python package, with patient sample included as a covariate to control for interpatient variability. For each gene, a Wald test was used to assess differential expression; multiple-testing correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the FDR. Genes with an adjusted P value (q value) below 0.05 were considered significantly differentially expressed.

Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the prerank function from the GSEApy Python package with 1,000 permutations. Before analysis, all genes were ranked according to their effect sizes (log-transformed fold changes) derived from the differential expression analysis. The following gene sets from previous studies were included. EMT gene sets: Wound response GO GP66, mesenchymal67, matrix remodelling68, TGFB activation (TGFB KEGG, TGFB CORE GENES/TGFB1/TGFB2)68,69, EMT activation (EMT Core Genes)67, EMT Hallmark70, pEMT71, EMT-II (MP13)72. SC gene sets: crypt base32, LGR5 intestinal SCs33, fetal8, regenerative34 and revival colonic SCs52. High-relapse gene sets: epithelial-specific high-risk gene set, core high-relapse cells73.

Trajectory analysis was performed using PAGA74 with the sc.tl.paga function built into Scanpy (v.1.9.6)75. To prepare the data, we first selected 3,000 highly variable genes using the seurat flavour of sc.pp.highly_variable_genes. Next, we calculated and selected 100 principal components (PCs) using sc.tl.pca. PCs were batch-corrected using Harmony (v.0.0.9)76 to correct for patient-specific gene expression profiles. Finally, nearest neighbours were calculated using sc.pp.neighbors (n_neighbors = 30) on the corrected PCs and PAGA was run on tumour architecture types.

In a recent development, we calculated diffusion pseudotime (DPT77) using the sc.tl.diffmap and sc.tl.dpt functions from Scanpy (v.1.9.6)75. In preparation, for a patient sample, we selected 3,000 highly variable genes using the seurat flavour of sc.pp.highly_variable_genes. Next, we calculated 100 principal components (PCs) using sc.tl.pca. Finally, nearest neighbours were calculated using sc.pp.neighbors (n_neighbors = 30) on the corrected PCs. DPT was run using a cell in the glandular region of the tumour as a ‘root cell’, representing its most unperturbed region.

According to recent reports, the use of human CRC organoid cultures was approved as part of the iCAN Precision Medicine Flagship study reviewed by the HUS Ethical Committee and is executed based on a HUS research permit (4.5.2023 §38 (HUS/223/2023)), a Findata data permit (THL/1338/14.02.00/2022) and material transfer agreements with Helsinki Biobank (HBP20210170) and Finnish Hematology and Registry Biobank FHRB (12.5.2022). The underlying PANORG study collecting the samples to the iCAN Flagship was approved by the ethical committee of the Helsinki and Uusimaa hospital district and study site institutional review boards (PANORG ethical approval HUS/390/2021, HUS approval HUS/69/2022). The study participants provided written, informed consent for the protocols. Organoids were maintained in a mixture of 60% LWRN medium (originally established in ref. 78) and 40% human basal medium supplemented with rhEGF (R&D, 236-EG, 100 ng ml−1); LWRN was replaced with Advanced DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for no-WNT conditions. Organoids were subjected to single-cell sequencing and selected to harbour APC and TP53 mutations for the studies here.

Patient-derived CRC organoids were cultured in Matrigel or collagen (drug treatment experiment), after which single-cell suspensions were generated by incubation with cell recovery solution (30 min at 4 °C; Corning) followed by digestion with TrypLE Express Enzyme (5 min at 37 °C; Invitrogen). After washing with ice-cold DMEM, single cells were counted using Luna-II automated cell counter (Logos Biosystems) and loaded on a microwell cartridge of the BD Rhapsody Express system (BD) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Single-cell whole-transcriptome analysis libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions using the BD Rhapsody WTA Reagent kit (BD, 633802) and sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 500 system using the High Output Kit v2.5 (150 cycles, Illumina) for 2 × 75 bp paired-end reads with 8 bp single index aiming sequencing depth of >20,000 reads per cell for each sample.

UMI, complex barcode, and sample tags were extracted from raw reads and demultiplexed using a custom script (rhapsody-demultiplex; https://github.com/Bioinformatics-Service-MPI-Munster/scrna-tools). Reads were mapped using STAR (v.2.7.10a)79 (--soloType CB_UMI_Complex --soloCellFilter None --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate --soloFeatures GeneFull_Ex50pAS --soloAdapterSequence NNNNNNNNNGTGANNNNNNNNNGACA --soloCBmatchWLtype 1MM --soloCBposition 2_0_2_8 2_13_2_21 3_1_3_9 --soloUMIposition 3_10_3_17 --soloCBwhitelist BD_CLS1_v2_draft.txt BD_CLS2_v2_draft.txt BD_CLS3_v2_draft.txt --runRNGseed 1 --soloMultiMappers EM --readFilesCommand zcat --outSAMattributes NH HI AS nM NM MD jM jI MC ch CB UB GX GN). Raw counts were imported as AnnData (v.0.10.7)80 objects in Python (v.3.9.11). We removed low-complexity barcodes using the knee plot method (1,500–3,000 counts per cell) and further filtered out cells with a high mitochondrial mRNA percentage (>50%). Doublets were predicted with scrublet (v.0.2.3)81. Finally, each sample’s gene expression matrix was normalized using scran (v.1.26.2)82, with Leiden clustering83 input at resolution 0.5.

At this stage, the samples were merged with scanpy (v.1.10.1)75. For 2D embedding, expression values were cell cycle regressed using sc.tl.score_genes_cell_cycle with G2M and S-phase gene lists from ref. 84 and sc.pp.regress_out. The expression matrix was subset to the 3,000 most highly variable genes (sc.pp.highly_variable_genes, flavor=“seurat”). We calculated and selected the top 100 PCs (sc.tl.pca), which served as basis for k-nearest neighbour calculation (sc.pp.neighbors, n_neighbors = 30). Nearest neighbours were then used as an input for UMAP layout (sc.tl.umap, min_dist = 0.3). Leiden clusters were calculated using sc.tl.leiden at resolution 0.7. Pseudotime and gene set enrichment analyses were performed as described for the spatial transcriptomics datasets. For reanalysis of the published tumour in vivo data, we chose a cell in the most stem-like cluster according to CytoTRACE analysis.

For generation of consensus gene sets, EMT gene sets (mesenchymal67, matrix remodelling68, TGFB activation (TGFB KEGG, TGFB CORE GENES/TGFB1/TGFB2)68,69, EMT activation (EMT Core Genes67, EMT Hallmark70, pEMT71, EMT-II (MP13)72) and SC gene sets (crypt base32, LGR5 intestinal SCs33, fetal8, regenerative34 and revival colonic SCs52) were merged and overlapping genes within and across gene sets were removed to generate the Core-EMT, Core-CBC and Core-RegSC gene sets.

All cells in the dataset were scored for the Core-EMT, Core-CBC and Core-RegSC gene sets using the Scanpy sc.tl.score_genes function. The scores were then converted to a per-dataset rank rescaled to [0, 1]. Cells were then ordered across the CBC to RegSC–EMT axis as a composite_trajectory = (RegSC_rank01 + EMT_rank01 − CBC_rank01 + 1)/3. Cells with composite_trajectory in the top 30% of the per-dataset distribution were classified hybrid.

For distribution across the EMT–RegSC axis, two curated marker panels were scored per hybrid cell with sc.tl.score_genes (random_state = 0): a RegSC-pole panel (GPRC5A, TSPAN1, PDZK1IP1, ANXA1, ANXA3, S100A6, S100A11, LCN2, SAA1, SAA2, KRT16, KRT17, SPP1, CD44, EMP1 and TACSTD2) and an EMT pole panel (SNAI1, SNAI2, ZEB1, ZEB2, TWIST1, TWIST2, VIM, FN1, S100A4, ACTA2, MMP14, PLAU, PLAUR, SERPINE1, TIMP1). Each panel score was z-scored within its dataset, and the pole axis was defined as axis_pole = z(score_EMT_pole) − z(score_RegSC_pole). The pole-axis shift among hybrid cells was computed as Cliff’s δ = 2 × U/(n_c × n_Unt) − 1, where U is the Mann–Whitney U statistic of axis pole over the two hybrid groups. δ ∈ [−1, +1]; δ < 0 represents that hybrid cells of c are shifted toward the regenerative pole relative to untreated-hybrid cells, δ > 0 represents that hybrid cells of c are shifted toward the EMT pole. By default, untreated sits at δ = 0.

Hydrogel scaffolds were engineered as described previously42,85. A PDMS stamp (see below) with a crypt-mimicking array of pillar topography was placed in the central top reservoir of the chip. To generate the ECM for the chip, bovine TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50mL, Advanced Biomatrix) was neutralized according to the manufacturer’s instructions and then mixed with Matrigel (356231, Corning) at a 75/25 (v/v) ratio. After gel injection through gel-loading port, hydrogel was polymerized at 37 °C, 5% CO2 (hereafter referred to as incubator) for 15 min. After ECM polymerization, all chip reservoirs were topped up with PBS or cell culture medium.

Stamps featuring crypt-mimicking microtopography were fabricated from PDMS by replica moulding of 2PP-printed models. First, arrays of colon crypt-mimicking micropillars were designed in Autodesk Fusion. Several topographies were tested and optimized, the final microtopography design consists of the slightly conical pillars, ranging from 50 to 120 µm in diameter (top to bottom) and 700 µm in height. The 3D model was printed using a NanoOne (UpNano) 2PP printer on glass coverslips with UpPhoto resin and a ×10/0.4 NA objective. To generate a master mould with inverted topography, the printed structures were plasma-activated and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning; 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio) was poured over the master, degassed under vacuum, and cured at 80 °C for 12 h. The resulting PDMS replica was cut, plasma-activated and silanized overnight as above. This PDMS negative was then used repeatedly as a mould for casting final PDMS stamps using the same procedure (Sylgard 184, 10:1 ratio, cured at 80 °C for 12 h).

Organoids were dissociated using TrypLE Express (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and resuspended at 40 million cells per ml in Advanced DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10 µM Y27632 after which 5 µl of cell suspension was plated onto each chip. Cells were allowed to settle for 1 h in a cell culture incubator, after which the chips were filled with Y27632-supplemented medium. The next day, Y27632 was removed and cells were cultured for 5 days. Chips were fixed in 4% PFA for 16 h at 4 °C, placed into 3D-printed custom histomoulds, filled with HistoGel (Thermo Fisher Scientific), embedded in paraffin and sectioned as described previously86. The samples were then processed for RNA in situ hybridization or immunofluorescence as described below.

In situ hybridization was performed using RNAscope technology (Advanced Cell Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. In brief, organoids were fixed in 4% PFA for 30 min at 37 °C, rinsed with PBS, dehydrated in a graded ethanol series and air dried. The slides were then rehydrated and 2 drops of hydrogen peroxide were added to each slide for 10 min. Primary antibodies were added and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The slides were washed and fixed with 4% PFA for 30 min at room temperature. After PBS washes, three drops of 1:15 diluted Protease Plus were added to slides and incubated for 10 min, followed by PBS washes.

Sources indicate that RNA probes were prewarmed for 10 min at 40 °C, cooled down and added onto slides. The slides were incubated with probes for 2 h at 40 °C, washed twice with wash buffer, subjected to stepwise hybridization with amplifier solutions for 15 min each at 40 °C, followed by application of blocker solutions. Finally, samples were incubated with Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies diluted in co-detection antibody diluent for 30 min at room temperature. After washes and brief incubation with DAPI, the slides were mounted in Elvanol and imaged. The following probes were used: ANXA1-c3 465411, LGR5-c2 311021, OLFM4-c1 311041, VIM-c1 310441. Images were obtained using the Zeiss LSM980 system using ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13).

Organoids were fixed in 4% PFA for 1 h at room temperature, permeabilized in 0.6% Triton X-100 for 30 min, blocked with 5% BSA and 5% goat serum in PBS for 2 h, after which primary antibodies were added in blocking solution and incubated overnight at 4 °C. After multiple washes in PBS, secondary Alexa Fluor-conjugated antibodies were added in 1% BSA, 1% goat serum for 2 h at room temperature. Organoids were then mounted in ProLong Gold (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The following primary antibodies were used: ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486, 1:1,000, overnight, 4 °C), YAP1 (Santa Cruz, sc-101199, 1:500, overnight, 4 °C), active YAP (Abcam, ab205270, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C), β-catenin (Cell Marque, 224M-14, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C), SNAIL1 (Santa Cruz, sc-271977, 1:50, overnight, 4 °C), HP1α (Cell Signaling, 2616, 1:200, overnight, 4 °C), lamin A/C (Cell Signaling, 2032, 1:200, overnight, 4 °C), SOX4 (Abcam, ab236557, 1:400, overnight, 4 °C), pSMAD2/3 (Cell Signaling, 3108, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C). Images were obtained using either the Zeiss LSM980 or Nikon Yokogawa CSU-W1 system with ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13) or NIS Elements (AR 5.41.01).

Recent findings suggest that to mechanically compress the organoids, organoids grown in Matrigel for 5 days were replated on top of Matrigel-coated 12–20 mm round glass coverslips and allowed to attach for 24 h. After attachment, the organoids were sandwiched with another 12–20 mm coverslip with a weight applying 200 Pa of vertical stress (generating a 45% reduction in organoid height) for 20 h.

Sources indicate that for 3D organoid imaging, single cells were first embedded in 8 mg ml−1 Matrigel and, after 4 days of culture, were transferred either to fresh Matrigel or pH-adjusted 1 mg ml−1 collagen I matrices. The organoids were treated with 5 µM TDI-011536 (MedChemExpress, HY-150042), 10 ng ml−1 TGFβ1 (StemCell Technologies, 78067.1) or both with daily medium replenishment while being live-cell imaged every 30 min with a Sartorius Incucyte S3 incubator microscope for up to 4 days.

Bright-field images were segmented using Cellpose4-SAM87 and edge detection followed by morphological gap-closing and hole-filling to obtain binary organoid masks that were imported to ImageJ (Fiji). MorphoLibJ88 was used to quantify convexity, Geodesic diameter, Geodesic elongation and organoid area that were scaled between 0 and 1 to initially classify the organoids into expanded, dispersive or cohesive classes in an unbiased manner. As the resolution of the masks was not sufficient to accurately capture surface structures, the classifications were all manually inspected further and assigned to the final classes.

Recent findings suggest that RNA was isolated using the NucleoSpin RNA plus Kit (Macherey-Nagel). RNA quality was assessed using the high-sensitivity RNA Screen Tape Analysis (TapeStation, Agilent) and subsequently 500 ng of RNA was reverse transcribed applying the SuperScript IV VILO Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. PCR was performed using the PowerUp SYBR Green Mastermix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on the QuantStudio5 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Gene expression was quantified using the ΔΔCt method with normalization to B2M. The following primers were used. B2M: forward primer, GAGTATGCCTGCCGTGTGAA; reverse primer, GCTTACATGTCTCGATCCCACT; AXIN2: forward primer, GCGCTGACGGATGATTCCAT; reverse primer, TGGGTTCTCGGGAAATGAGGT; ASCL2: forward primer, CGCCTACTCGTCGGACGACAG; reverse primer, GCCGCTCGCTCGGCTTCCG.

Recent findings suggest that mouse colonoscopy was performed using the TELE PACK+VET system (Karl Storz, RP101S1). Illumination was provided by a xenon light source connected through the Adapt. KST fibre-optic light cable/Xenon 100 (495KS). The system includes a camera control, air insufflation units and an integrated endoscopic video unit with built-in documentation and memory storage. Colonoscopy imaging was performed using an integrated multipurpose Hopkins Telescope (67031BA) with an outer diameter of 11.5 Fr. Images were acquired using an IMAGE1 S HX FULL HD Camera Head (TH110). Mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane and organoid fragments corresponding to 5 × 105 single cells were transplanted into the colonic submucosa using a Hamilton syringe (Hamilton, Reno, 7656-01) equipped with a transfer needle for sample loading (7770-02) and an injection needle (7803-05). The needle was carefully inserted into the colonic submucosa, and 50 µl of organoid fragments suspended in 1 mg ml−1 rat collagen type 1 (Sigma-Aldrich, C3867) supplemented with 10% Corning Matrigel (Corning, 356231) was delivered and generated a visible submucosal bleb. The mice were treated for 5 days after transplantation with the LATS kinase inhibitor TDI-011536 (MedChemExpress, HY-150042). TDI-011536 was prepared at a concentration of 5 mg ml−1 by emulsification in 10% Kolliphor HS 15 (Merck, 42966) in PBS and administered by oral gavage twice daily at a dose of 2.5 mg per kg. Vehicle-treated animals received 10% Kolliphor in PBS alone.

TGFβ1 treatment was performed using human recombinant TGFβ1 (StemCell Technologies, 78067.1) within Affi-Gel Blue beads (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 153-7301). In brief, beads were washed four times with ice-cold bi-distilled water and incubated overnight with 500 µl of 50 µg ml−1 TGFβ1 in PBS supplemented with 10 mM HEPES. TGFβ1-loaded beads were mixed with organoid fragments in collagen solution at a final proportion of 10% (v/v) before implantation. For dual-treatment experiments, animals received both TDI-011536 administration and TGFβ1-loaded beads as described above. Each treatment group consisted of four mice (n = 4). Mice were monitored three times per week, and colonoscopy imaging was performed every 2 weeks for 4 weeks before euthanasia.

Tissue biopsies (intestinal rolls) were fixed in 4% PFA, embedded in paraffin and sectioned. Sections were de-paraffinized using a graded alcohol series and antigen retrieval was carried out using target retrieval solution (Dako) at pH 6 or pH 9 in a pressure cooker. Unspecific binding was blocked using 5% normal goat serum, 3% BSA in PBS, after which antibodies were diluted in DAKO antibody diluent and incubated overnight in a moist chamber at 4 °C. After PBS washes, Alexa-Fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies were diluted in 1% BSA in PBS, incubated for 1 h at room temperature, after which samples were mounted in Elvanol. The following primary antibodies were used: ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486), pSMAD2/3 (Cell Signaling, 3108) and active YAP (Abcam ab205270). Images were obtained using the Zeiss LSM980 system with ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13). The tumour area was quantified using ANXA1 staining to generate a ROI mask in Fiji. The number of ROIs was used to extract the lesion number.

All animal experiments were performed in accordance with EU Directive 2010/63/EU and Finnish legislation, and were approved by the National Animal Experiment Board of Finland (ELLA) under project licence ESAVI/30305/2023. Female NOD.Cg-PrkdcscidIl2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 005557) were used at 12 weeks of age at the start of the experiment. Sample size was determined using the resource equation method (E = N − T), where N is the total number of animals and T the number of groups; with four groups of four mice (N = 16), E = 12, within the recommended range of 10–20. Mice were randomly allocated to experimental groups; no formal randomization method was used. Tumour implantation was confirmed in all mice, and animals were euthanized and dissected 4 weeks after transplantation. No mice reached the humane end-point limits defined in the licence, and no mice were excluded from the analysis.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad, v.9) or in R (v.2023.09.1+494). Statistical significance was determined using the specific tests indicated in the corresponding figure legends. Only two-tailed tests were used. In all cases in which a test for normally distributed data was used, normal distribution was confirmed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (α = 0.05). All experiments presented in the manuscript were repeated at least in three independent replicates. Automated software algorithms were used for unbiased quantification of staining intensities, sequencing data and architecture features/cell shapes in all experiments involving these techniques so blinding was not relevant. For animal experiments endoscopy and sample collection were performed in a blinded manner. For manual organoid invasion pattern classification blinding was applied during data analysis. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. Sample size was determined based on previous experience, published literature, or to specific requirements of a given technique.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

In a recent development, the single-cell sequencing data are available at the GEO (GSE297054 and GSE333618). Spatial transcriptomics data have been uploaded to Keeper (https://keeper.mpdl.mpg.de/d/4033948ddc0b4e06aaeb/). All patient-related data (TMA and spatial transcriptomics post-hoc staining) have been deposited in the Helsinki Biobank (HBP20210170) and Finnish Hematology and Registry Biobank FHRB (12.5.2022). The pretrained U-Net model is available in ONNX format at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20343193)89. All in vitro data are available from the authors on request. Latest Update: Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick

📅 25 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 30 min read (6009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~30 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated.
  • The former midfielder will carry the can.
  • Recent findings suggest that more than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

Recent findings suggest that more than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

According to recent reports, an announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

Industry observers note that that is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

According to recent reports, if it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

In a recent development, at 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

In a recent development, the television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Industry observers note that finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a latest manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Sources indicate that bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the latest head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

What a finish from Rayan to give Bournemouth the lead! 🔥 https://t.co/9BV0G5Tqgi.

Recent findings suggest that the outstanding Rayan should have had a hat-trick but failed to take two chances in the second half, when he only had goalkeeper Senne Lammens to beat, after Bournemouth had already doubled their lead. It came as Leny Yoro slipped over and presented the ball straight to Adrien Truffert, who squared it for Marcus Tavernier to side-foot home. It was that ridiculously easy.

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

Recent findings suggest that with just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

Industry observers note that is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

Industry observers note that at the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I noted here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location.".

Recent findings suggest that german Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

Recent findings suggest that given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz said when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

In a recent development, the economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

According to recent reports, "The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," remarked Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending.".

The chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that.".

According to recent reports, but these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she remarked.

The government is presently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in fresh debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

However, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," remarked Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, mentioned the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.

It has been revealed that according to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz mentioned there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a tech giant can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

According to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

In a recent development, if the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it remarked in the report. "Upcoming technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop.".

But innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

Sources indicate that upcoming evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

The intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a new study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association highlighted that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

A smile did eventually spread across the face of Erling Haaland when dissecting Manchester City’s draw with Napoli, stretching their worrying run to one victory in five games.

Industry observers note that not for the first time in recent weeks, he had appeared morose and despondent, radiating an air of gloom, talking about how the team are ‘questioning anything’ amid these results. That’s not exactly inspiring confidence among their supporters.

But just as City’s captain for the night was about to finish his media duties before heading home, one final question focused on Sunday’s clash with Arsenal and a rivalry with a ‘certain centre half’. Haaland’s mood changed instantly.

‘It's always good to play against the best teams,’ mentioned the Norwegian, breaking out into a smirk as he allowed the impending battle with Gabriel to percolate.

‘Arsenal were the best team last year and one of the best in the last five years now, so it's fun to play against them and it’s always fun to play against Gabriel.’.

There was, at last, some positive emotion. Is Gabriel and that playground scrapping what he needs to re-energise? We’ll find out in a few days.

Erling Haaland appeared morose and despondent following Man City's draw with Napoli, suggesting he was 'questioning everything' amid their worrying run of form.

Haaland did raise a smile about the prospect of his impending battle with Arsenal defender Gabriel this weekend.

The Man City star has shown increasing dejected body language during games and has spent too much time recently with his head bowed and hand waving at team-mates.

Haaland talked about City needing to be at their maximum to take anything from the Emirates this weekend. Whether that is ‘fun’ or not is a different matter entirely, but what Enzo Maresca must demand more from all of his players. Even with 14 goals already this term, that includes Haaland.

He is leading from the front off the pitch. Standing in front of the cameras more than anyone else, facing up to the dipping form and taking on those responsibilities without complaining. The forward wrote on X on Wednesday afternoon: 'Together through the ups and downs. Thank you for pushing us until the very end yesterday. Full focus on Sunday now.'.

Yet City need more of that leadership between the white lines from somebody who has drawn a blank in four of his last five club matches, despite scoring three times over the international break.

There is too much head bowing and hand waving at the moment.

The 26-year-old admits he has to give extra. And believes that the team are generally creating enough chances for him, even if the freewheeling attacking abandon of early season has vanished.

Industry observers note that city's results are clearly affecting Haaland’s mood and that can be self-perpetuating. He admits that failing to reverse this run is hurting him. That is evident by watching his increasingly dejected body language during games and the frustration seen when he gestured at Abdukodir Khusanov as the defender dithered with a routine throw-in during Saturday’s draw against Fulham. It wasn’t the picture of a man happy with his lot.

Industry observers note that only Haaland will know whether that general angst is contributing to a lack of intensity in his own performances. Nobody has mentioned the striker carrying a knock, although Maresca has appeared focused on offering him rest whenever possible over the past three months.

Something is undoubtedly proving an obstacle for him. He’s insisted that it isn’t the guilty verdicts hanging over City and, listening to him, the gripes and disappointment look focused on City’s lack of control in games. It also cannot help that Haaland will feel aggrieved to have seen a goal on Saturday chalked off for a foul on Bernd Leno and then to have not been awarded a penalty for grappling on Tuesday night.

If both or even one of those decisions go his way, the interview that sparked concern with fans – one conducted almost immediately after full time when emotions are at their highest – would likely have been very different.

It has been revealed that city will have to cling on to the idea that a sullen Haaland is at least a Haaland who cares. And a Haaland who cares must surely dig them out of this hole, even if he cannot do that alone.

Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 101 min read (20110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~101 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, although coronary artery disease (CAD) genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci, most variants lie in non-coding regions, obscuring the causal gene programmes and cell types driving disease1,2.
  • Common diseases are driven by a multitude of factors and remain difficult to treat given the lack of a unified disease mechanism4.
  • Although population-scale GWAS offer great opportunity for target discovery, most identified variants lie within non-coding regions of the genome, making it difficult to dissect the causal cell types and molecular pathways13.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, although coronary artery disease (CAD) genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci, most variants lie in non-coding regions, obscuring the causal gene programmes and cell types driving disease1,2. Here we performed single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility in human coronary arteries from 44 people to construct a genome-wide single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map. We identified 11,269 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) across principal vascular cell types, including CAD-associated caQTLs in smooth muscle cells (SMCs). Using dynamic single-cell caQTL modelling3, we show that variant effects on chromatin vary across SMC states. For example, rs658956-mediated suppression of the FGGY-DT enhancer through disruption of an AP-1 motif is amplified as SMCs transition towards a fibromyocyte fate. We next performed genome-wide high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) in 15 human coronary arteries, showing that rs4887091 in the ADAMTS7 CAD locus has allele-dependent effects on CCCTC-binding factor occupancy and loop strength. Integrating Hi-C, Hi-C with chromatin immunoprecipitation and in vitro clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats interference (CRISPRi) nominated AMOTL2 as a distal SMC-specific CAD gene whose loss promotes proliferation and suppresses contractile identity. Finally, arrayed Perturb–seq of GWAS-nominated enhancers converged on extracellular matrix remodelling as a core SMC disease programme. Together, these findings provide a framework for mapping non-coding GWAS variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

Common diseases are driven by a multitude of factors and remain difficult to treat given the lack of a unified disease mechanism4. Coronary artery disease (CAD) is among the most prevalent common chronic diseases, and numerous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have now identified hundreds of variants linked to CAD risk. Although these results may potentially pave the way for new therapeutic target discovery1,2,5,6, much of the translation from GWAS to therapeutic targets for CAD has been restricted to lipid-lowering drugs7,8. Large-scale clinical studies have demonstrated a persistent residual risk of CAD independent of lipid levels9,10, but we lack drugs that directly target disease pathways in the vessel wall due to an incomplete understanding of causal disease mechanisms. Leveraging human genetics to uncover new lipid-independent biological mechanisms and drug targets in CAD represents a tremendous unmet need and would be a principal milestone in translating population-scale GWAS findings to therapies for patients11,12.

Although population-scale GWAS offer great opportunity for target discovery, most identified variants lie within non-coding regions of the genome, making it difficult to dissect the causal cell types and molecular pathways13. The advent of single-cell sequencing technologies now allows for the profiling of human tissues in health and disease at unprecedented granularity14. Previous studies have used traditional single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) for detailed characterization of cell states in human tissue that drive disease15,16,17,18; however, these studies do not profile the non-coding genome, making it challenging to link GWAS variants to observed molecular changes. More recently, single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) with sequencing (snATAC–seq) in human coronary arteries was conducted to link CAD GWAS variants to regulatory elements19. Although this represented an important advance in the field, the lack of complementary transcriptomic profiling rendered it challenging to nominate causal genes in vascular cell types. Furthermore, isolated snATAC–seq precludes the discovery of distal gene regulation as a driver of disease20, and there are right now no studies that profile the three-dimensional (3D) chromatin architecture in human coronary arteries to enable the investigation of these distal regulatory connections.

Recent findings suggest that herein we performed simultaneous multi-omic profiling of the transcriptome and epigenome in nuclei from 44 human coronary arteries to build a multi-omic enhancer–gene map of CAD. Collectively, these analyses identified CAD-associated regulatory variants and enhancer–gene links in smooth muscle cells (SMCs), motivating focused analysis of SMC state-dependent gene regulation. To expand insight into gene regulation across functionally heterogeneous SMC cell states, we used dynamic chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTL) modelling to uncover cell-state-dependent pathogenicity of disease variants. To dissect the role of disease-associated variants in regulating larger scale gene networks, we performed genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries to link variants to distal genes and validated our findings using cell-specific high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) with chromatin immunoprecipitation (Hi-ChIP–seq) and in vitro CRISPRi. Finally, we performed Perturb–seq in human coronary artery SMCs (HCASMCs) to characterize functional mechanisms of repressing disease-associated enhancers and genes. Collectively, we provide a multi-omic map of human CAD by integrating transcriptomic, epigenetic and chromatin architecture to link disease-associated genetic variants with candidate disease-relevant cell types and target genes.

Sources indicate that we performed single-nucleus Multi-ome (RNA+ATAC) sequencing in 44 human coronary arteries from non-failing donors and patients with chronic heart failure isolated at the time of heart transplantation (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). After quality control, we recovered 126,804 nuclei from 11 distinct cell types (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 1b–d). Using differential expression of canonical genes, we identified clusters corresponding to all main vascular cell types, including coronary artery SMCs (MYH11, ACTA2, ITGA8), endothelial cells (VWF, LDB2, PECAM1), fibroblasts (LAMA2, DCN, FBLN1) and myeloid cells (F13A1, CD163, MRC1) (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Table 2). We used MACS2 to identify areas of open chromatin (‘peaks’) from the ATAC–seq data (Fig. 1e) and identified 143,743 cell-type-specific differentially accessible peaks (Extended Data Fig. 1d,e). Generally, cell-type clustering was concordant between the RNA and ATAC data. However, gene-expression data enabled the annotation of rarer cell types that were not captured by ATAC-based clustering alone (Supplementary Fig. 1e–g). Using differentially accessible peaks across cells, we also discovered cell-type-specific enrichment of transcriptional motifs such as SpiB and PU.1 in myeloid cells, MEF2B/C/D in SMCs and CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein in adipocytes (Supplementary Fig. 1h). We linked peaks to genes using a newly introduced supervised single-cell model called single-cell enhancer-to-gene (E2G) (scE2G)21 (Fig. 1d, Extended Data Fig. 2a–g and Supplementary Tables 3–14; Methods). We found that the non-immune cells had the greatest number of shared enhancers relative to myeloid cells (Fig. 1d) and that all cell types had a similar number of E2G links (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 3).

a, Study design. b, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding plot of integrated data clustered by RNA. c, Cell-type composition stack plot by sample. NK, natural killer. d, Number of shared enhancers heatmap (right) from scE2G map (left); defined as the number of enhancers where more than 50% of the peak width overlaps with other cell type-specific peaks. e, Number of scE2G links in the main cell types. f, Linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) for cardiometabolic traits by cell type; dotted line, multiple-testing-adjusted P value threshold. P values were calculated using one-sided stratified LDSC, with Bonferroni correction for six conditions (P < 8.33 × 10−3). Illustrations in a and d created in BioRender: a, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/ib7ak3x (2026); d, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/cwi31gk (2026).

In a recent development, notably, we found that cardiometabolic disease variants for CAD, systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were enriched in differentially accessible marker peaks specific to SMCs and endothelial cells (Fig. 1f). As a predominantly non-vascular trait, diabetes did not demonstrate enrichment of disease-associated variants (Fig. 1f).

To boost our power for single-cell caQTL (sc-caQTL) discovery, we integrated our Multi-ome ATAC–seq data with available snATAC–seq data from human coronary arteries19 to create a meta-map of 88 samples and 245,562 nuclei across four ancestry groups (Extended Data Fig. 3a–f). We then used RASQUAL to identify pseudobulk caQTLs in four principal vascular cell types (SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells, fibroblasts) (Fig. 2a). At the 10% false discovery rate (FDR) threshold, we found 11,269 significant caQTL associations in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3g–i, Supplementary Fig. 2a–d and Supplementary Tables 15–26). Power, sensitivity, subsampling and runtime analyses are shown in Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3 and described in Supplementary Methods.

In a recent development, a, Schematic of sc-caQTL discovery with disease enrichment. b, Number of sc-caQTLs by cell type at FDR 0.05. c, Regional Manhattan plot of CAD GWAS1 and SMC caQTL results at the rs658956 locus. d, snATAC–seq tracks with E2G link centred at the rs658956 locus showing SMC-specific enrichment of the enhancer with an E2G link to FGGY-DT. e, Violin plot showing normalized expression by genotype for rs658956 and FGGY-DT in coronary arteries from GTEx (P = 3.39 × 10−12). The P value was calculated using a two-sided t-test of the GTEx eQTL linear regression coefficient against zero. f, PRINT and seq2PRINT transcription factor binding prediction pipeline (left). rs658956 overlaps region with high transcription factor binding probability from seq2PRINT model (top) and multiscale footprinting associates rs658956 with a transcription factor-specific footprint (bottom). g, Motif analysis finds rs658956 overlaps canonical AP-1 transcription factor (JUN, FOS) motifs. Ref, reference alelle; Alt, alternate allele. h, EMSA demonstrates a binding shift in the reference allele sequence (containing G) that was not present in the alternative allele sequence (containing T) when these allelic sequences were exposed to nuclear lysate from SMCs (n = 3 replicates, representative experiment shown). i, Dynamic caQTL modelling and discovery strategy (cell-state-dependent). j, rs658956 caQTL dynamic effect size. Net effect size depicted here represents the sum of \({\beta }_{g}\) and \({\beta }_{{\rm{F}}{\rm{M}}{\rm{C}}{\rm{x}}{\rm{G}}}\) in our generalized linear mixed model across cells. k, rs658956 genotype association with normalized chromatin accessibility across FMC tertiles. Negative slope of association increases as FMC score increases; n = 268 (e) and n = 79 (k) biologically independent samples were used. Illustrations in a and i created in BioRender: a, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/cwi31gk (2026); i, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/m3r2gap (2026).

In a recent development, we further characterized caQTL variants to assess their regulatory potential. Lead caQTL variants were enriched strongly near the peaks they were predicted to regulate, consistent with a cis-regulatory mechanism (Extended Data Fig. 3j). We next overlapped our pseudobulk caQTLs and GTEx bulk arterial tissue eQTLs by cell type and found several hundred shared QTL variants in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3i). Furthermore, we found a strong correlation in effect size between our SMC caQTLs and bulk coronary artery eQTLs from GTEx (Extended Data Fig. 3k). Finally, in SMCs we trained a convolutional neural net model (seq2PRINT22) that incorporates chromatin accessibility and ATAC footprinting to predict transcription factor binding probability at a base-pair resolution. We found that caQTL variants within accessible peaks had significantly higher predicted transcription factor binding probabilities compared with all other non-caQTL SNP sites within accessible peaks (P = 8.2 × 10−40, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Extended Data Fig. 3l).

To identify disease-associated caQTLs, we overlapped sc-caQTLs for each cell type with CAD GWAS variants (defined as lead variants associated with CAD at 1% FDR1 and variants in linkage disequilibrium with these at R2 ≥ 0.8 in the European population from 1000 Genomes Project; Supplementary Table 27), which yielded numerous disease-relevant cell-type-specific caQTLs (Extended Data Fig. 3m). For example, we found that rs7182567 was an SMC-specific caQTL that was also a GWAS variant (P = 5.4 × 10−26) and a bulk GTEx eQTL for ADAMTS7 in tibial artery (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Similarly, we found that rs8017642 is an endothelial cell-specific caQTL in the NEK9 locus (Extended Data Fig. 4b), whereas rs2337154 and rs1443120 are fibroblast- and myeloid-specific caQTLs, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d).

Next, we leveraged the paired RNA data to sub-cluster SMCs into transcriptionally distinct cell states, forming a continuum from ‘healthy’ contractile SMC states (SMC1–3) to de-differentiated ‘disease-associated’ SMC states including fibromyocytes (FMCs) and chondromyocytes (CMCs) (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Notably, we found that ADAMTS7 was expressed most highly in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 4e), indicating a role in disease regulation. To identify functionally distinct endothelial cell states, we mapped our data to a high-resolution scRNA-seq atherosclerosis atlas23 and identified four transcriptionally distinct endothelial subsets (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Notably, NEK9 was expressed in endothelial cells enriched with endothelium-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes such as COL1A1 and FN1 (refs. 24,25) (Extended Data Fig. 4f,g). Pathway enrichment in the EMT population showed increased EMT and stress-response signals (Extended Data Fig. 4h). Next, we created a gene set score comprised of 41 endothelial cell-specific genes thought to be associated causally with CAD26 that showed maximal enrichment in intimal endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Similarly, we created a gene signature of a gene programme26 identified previously as driving CAD pathogenesis in endothelial cells (Programme 8) and found an enrichment of this programme in angiogenic and/or vasa vasorum endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4j).

Recent findings suggest that the CAD disease-associated variant rs658956 illustrates how a cell-type-specific caQTL can impart functional transcriptional changes. The variant is an SMC-specific and fibroblast-specific caQTL and regulates a putative enhancer element (chr. 1: 59169569–59170069), which is linked to the gene FGGY-DT in an SMC-specific manner by scE2G (Fig. 2c,d). Consistently, we found that rs658956 is also a coronary artery eQTL for FGGY-DT expression (P = 3.4 × 10−12) wherein the alternative allele (T) is associated with decreased expression relative to the reference allele (G) (Fig. 2e) and is also predicted to overlie a high probability transcription factor binding site (Fig. 2f). Motif-based transcription factor binding site analysis found that rs658956 is predicted to disrupt a core AP-1 (JUN/FOS) transcription factor binding motif (5′-TGAGTCA-3′) (Fig. 2g). Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) demonstrated a binding shift in the reference allele sequence (containing G) that was not present in the alternative allele sequence (containing T) when these alleles were exposed to nuclear lysate from SMCs (Fig. 2h). Antibody supershift EMSA confirmed that the shifted AP-1 complex band consists of JUN and FOS transcription factors (Extended Data Fig. 4k). Together, these results suggest that the disease-associated variant rs658956 impacts transcription factor binding, thereby decreasing the chromatin accessibility of the enhancer and subsequently reducing FGGY-DT expression in a SMC-specific manner.

It has been revealed that in atherosclerosis, SMCs undergo a well-characterized phenotypic switch from a contractile state to a fibroblast-like FMC phenotype16, driven by disease-associated transcriptional programmes. To characterize this transition, individual nuclei were assigned an FMC score based on FMC state marker genes for downstream modelling (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 5a–d). Notably, this FMC gene score is dynamic with disease across species, disease burden, pseudotime trajectory, in vitro HCASMC stress and transcriptional regulation (Extended Data Fig. 5e–k). To identify state-dependent caQTL effects, we used a Poisson mixed-effects (PME) single-cell model (Extended Data Fig. 6a–c; Methods). Applying this PME model to the lead variants of SMC-specific pseudobulk caQTLs, we identified 712 caQTLs whose effects were dynamic with respect to the FMC score (FDR ≤ 5%) (Supplementary Tables 29 and 30). Notably, eight of these dynamic caQTLs were also disease-associated variants. For example, rs658956 exhibited a significant interaction with FMC score (FDR-adjusted likelihood ratio test (LRT) P value = 2.36 × 10−4) (Fig. 2j,k). A negative interaction term indicates that, as the FMC score increased, the negative association between rs658956 and local chromatin accessibility was amplified (Fig. 2j,k). Using the scE2G map to link dynamic caQTL-related enhancer elements (caPeaks) to target genes, we found that extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling was the most enriched pathway among linked genes (Extended Data Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Table 31). Notably, several of these genes linked to dynamic caPeaks were enriched in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 32). Similar state-dependent effects were observed at other CAD loci such as dynamic caQTL variant rs11838776 in the COL4A1 locus, suggesting that COL4A1 may play a role during transition toward an FMC state (Extended Data Fig. 6g–k). Collectively, these dynamic analyses demonstrate that disease-associated variants can exert cell-state-dependent regulatory effects on chromatin accessibility.

To map CAD disease-associated variants to cell types and genes in an unbiased fashion, we built a disease-relevant single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map (scV2E2G) integrating cell-type-specific regulatory elements, CAD GWAS variants, scE2G links and caQTLs21,27 (Fig. 3a; Methods).
